Learning Objectives
Identify common causes of axial low back pain in adults.
Review anatomic, biomechanical, and cellular factors that contribute to low back pain in
general, degenerative disk disease, and facet degeneration.
Apply important physical examination findings and diagnostic considerations in evaluating
patients with low back pain.
Determine nonsurgical and surgical treatment options for patients with symptomatic
degenerative disk disease.
Compare outcome studies on the management of degenerative disk disease via fusion and
total disk replacement.

Overview
Axial low back pain (LBP) is defined as pain in the lumbar or lumbosacral area that does not
radiate into the lower extremities.1
Direct correlation with anatomic structures or pathologic conditions is not always possible.
In general, most LBP is multifactorial, being related to mechanical, neurophysiologic, and/or
psychologic factors.

Overview
LBP may result from a myriad of spinal (Table 1) and extraspinal (Table 2) causes.
Lumbar degenerative disk disease (DDD) followed by painful facet joints are the most
common causes of axial LBP in adults2 (Resource 1). In most patients, these conditions
can be successfully managed nonsurgically via physical therapy, medications, and
lifestyle modifications. Surgical treatment for patients with DDD in whom nonsurgical
treatment fails traditionally involved fusion of the affected spinal segment to eliminate
motion and the associated pain. An alternative to fusion is replacement of the painful
disk via total disk replacement (TDR).

Epidemiology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000052
4/41

As many as 85% of all individuals will experience LBP at some point in their lives.3,4 The annual
incidence of LBP in adults is 15%. LBP has an annual prevalence of 38% and represents a
substantial socioeconomic burden, with costs exceeding $100 billion per year in the United
States alone.5,6 LBP is the second most common reason, after the common cold, patients visit
a physician.7,8
DDD is a common cause of chronic LBP in adults. Some evidence of disk degeneration is
observed on the imaging studies of as many as one-third of asymptomatic individuals.
Abnormal lumbar findings are observed on MRIs in almost all individuals older than 60 years.3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
An understanding of spine anatomy is critical in identifying causes of LBP
9
(Resource 2).
A functional spinal unit consists of the intervertebral disk, cranially and caudally adjacent
vertebral bodies, and associated paired facet joints.
The disk consists of the outer anulus fibrosus and the inner nucleus pulposus.

Osteology
Lumbar vertebrae have large, rectangular bodies with nonoverlapping spinous
processes. Usually, five mobile, non–rib-bearing vertebrae are present; however,
variability is common. Sacralization of L5 occurs in approximately 2% to 15% of
individuals. Conversely, lumbarization of S1 is observed in 3% to 7% of individuals.
The sacrum is a single structure composed of the five embryologic sacral vertebrae. The
sacrum contains four sacral foramina through which the sacral nerve roots pass. The S5
roots run though the sacral hiatus.
The intervertebral disks and vertebral bodies support 80% of the axial load through the
spine. The anulus of the disk is a fibrous layer consisting of obliquely oriented type I
collagen molecules. The softer nucleus is a remnant of the embryologic notochord and is
composed of type II collagen molecules. It functions as a force cushion by converting
axial loads into radially directed forces in the surrounding anulus via hydrostatic force.

9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000052
5/41

Tears in the anulus (anular fissure) and internal disk disruption with progressive
degeneration may contribute to discogenic pain.
Vasculature
Retroperitoneal vascular anatomy is relevant to anterior and lateral approaches used in the
management of DDD (Resource 3).
Bifurcation of the iliac vessels typically occurs at L4. The inferior vena cava (IVC) is on the right
side of the spine.
The descending aorta is to the left of the IVC.
Nerves
The lumbar nerve roots exit the spinal canal bilaterally below the corresponding pedicle. For
example, the bilateral L5 nerve roots exit below the L5 pedicle.
Joints and Ligaments
Also called zygapophyseal joints, the paired facet joints are the articulating components of the
functional spinal unit. The orientation of facet joints varies throughout the spine and
corresponds with the amount and direction of motion.
Facet joint anatomy is similar to that of other synovial joints in the body, with articular cartilage
covering subchondral bone.
In a healthy lumbar spine, the facet joints share 20% of the axial load.
Stress across the joint increases in extension and decreases in flexion.

Joints and Ligaments
The lumbar facet joints allow approximately 50° of coronal motion and 90° of sagittal
motion. Overgrowth of the superior facet of the caudal vertebrae is the main offending
structure in patients with lumbar foraminal stenosis. For example, the L5 superior
articular facet is the offending structure at L4/5.

Musculature
The lumbar intrinsic musculature is important for spinal stabilization and consists of the
erector spinae muscles (medial to lateral: spinalis, longissimus, and iliocostalis) and the
multifidus muscles.

Musculature
The longissimus muscles originate on the lumbar transverse processes and insert along
the iliac crest. The iliocostalis muscles originate more lateral on the transverse process
and insert along the thoracolumbar fascia and the iliac crest. The multifidus muscles
arise from the spinous processes and insert on the on the mamillary process of
vertebrae two to four levels caudal.
Etiology
The three most common causes of axial LBP in adults are the intervertebral disk (40%), the
lumbar facet joint (15% to 30%), and the sacroiliac joint (20%).2
The exact cause of DDD is unclear; however, numerous factors have been identified as
contributors to LBP (Resource 4). Age- or injury-related degenerative changes at the disk alter
the flow of nutrients into the disk. This alters the ability of the disk to respond to physiologic
loads.10
Changes in disk water content, the disruption of aggrecan and collagen within the disk, and the
alteration of the flow of nutrients into the disk alter the ability of the disk to respond to
pathologic processes.
The relationship between LBP and DDD is not completely understood. For example, two
patients with similar degrees of DDD may have substantial variation in symptoms.
Excessive loads and injury to the disk result in the expression of catabolic enzymes, such as
collagenases and matrix metalloproteinases.11
Facet joint degenerative osteoarthritis is the most frequent form of facet joint pain.
The intrinsic musculature of the of the spine may contribute to axial LBP.


Etiology
Historically, vertebral disks were thought to be relatively avascular and aneural. Although
the nucleus pulposus is aneural, the outer anulus fibrosus contains nociceptive fibers
from the ventral ramus and the sinuvertebral nerve as well as the gray ramus
communicans. Injured or inflamed disks also may acquire additional pain fibers. Neural
hypersensitivity and neurovascular ingrowth to the disk occur in response to neural
mediators (nitric oxide, phospholipase A2, glutamate, substance P, calcitonin gene-
related peptide).12 Regardless of the cause, disk degeneration is characterized by a local
increase in the production of proinflammatory cytokines.
Normal age-related degenerative changes are different than painful, symptomatic DDD.
The multifactorial changes that occur in disk morphology with aging include mechanical,
traumatic, and nutritional accumulated changes resulting in loss of disk height,
osteophyte formation, and changes in the anulus fibrosus. Symptomatic DDD is believed
to result from failure of the nucleus pulposus to effectively disperse load and
accompanying anular fissuring and bone marrow changes in the end plate. Damage to
the disk structures leads to pathologic load dispersion. This, in combination with altered
nociception caused by cytokines, leads to discogenic pain.
Granulation tissue forms in the anular defects, which contain vascular and nervous
tissue. Recently, some studies have questioned whether indolent bacterial infections
lead to chronic inflammation and, eventually, chronic LBP.13
Loss of disk height also results in stress concentration at the endplate cartilage and the
vertebral body, leading to degeneration of these structures as well. Reduced disk height
alters the loading characteristics of the facet joints. Over time, the facet joint capsules
may become incompetent, leading to increased motion and subsequent facet joint
degeneration and hypertrophy. Facet hypertrophy, particularly of the superior articular
process, may lead to compression of the neural elements (Figure 1).

Figure 1 T2-weighted midsagittal (A) and L3-L4 axial (B and C) MRIs of a spine show
central and lateral recess stenosis from L3 to L5. Note facet hypertrophy and
ligamentum flavum redundancy (more visible on panel B) causing central and lateral
recess stenosis. (Reproduced from Mroz TE, Steinmetz MP: Lumbar degenerative disease

Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 173-188.)
Similar to other synovial joints, osteoarthritic facet changes include loss of joint space,
narrowing, loss of synovial fluid, loss of cartilage, and bony overgrowth. High-grade
cartilage necrosis occurs rapidly within the facets.
Although extremely rare, septic facet arthritis can occur, most commonly in patients with
other spinal infection (osteomyelitis discitis). Facet joint arthritis also may occur in
patients with inflammatory arthropathies, such as rheumatoid arthritis.
The most common type of muscular LBP results from overuse and rapid muscle
lengthening. Micro-tears in the muscle in combination with lactic acid–associated
chemical irradiation are perceived by receptors within the muscle.10 In general,
muscular LBP is self-limiting.
Natural History
Most episodes of acute LBP resolve within a few weeks without management.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000052
9/41

DDD usually begins in the third decade of life.
L4/5 and L5/S1 are the most commonly affected levels.
Patients with discogenic pain report a deep ache in their low back rather than the sharp or
burning pain characteristic of radiculopathy.

Natural History
Progressive degeneration of a spinal motion segment was classically described by
Kirkaldy-Willis as dysfunction followed by instability followed by stabilization.14 The
stabilization that occurs is to the result of osteophyte formation between adjacent
bodies. The disk and the endplate cartilage become fibrotic, and motion is largely lost.15
Risk Factors
Smoking, increased age, diabetes mellitus, infection, depression, certain genetic factors, and
obesity increase the risk of LBP and disk degeneration.
Smoking, diabetes mellitus, and vascular disease decrease already low oxygen tension within
the disk, leading to an abundance of catabolic metabolism.
Although rare, DDD may be observed in adolescents, likely as a result of genetic/anatomic
predisposition.
Classification
No formal classification systems for LBP or DDD exist; however, LBP is frequently
differentiated by chronicity because the natural history, management, and prognosis change.
Acute LBP is defined as functionally limiting back pain that lasts less than 3 months. Chronic
LBP is defined as pain that lasts for more than 3 months. Typically, patients with acute LBP
have nonspecific symptoms without neurologic deficits. The episode often is self-limiting, and
a cause rarely is identified.
Two classification systems for facet joint degeneration are recommended for clinical use.
The radiographic-based Pathria classification of facet degeneration includes three grades.16
Grade 1: facet joint narrowing
Grade 2: facets with narrowing and sclerosis or hypertrophy

Grade 3: facets with severe degenerative disease, including narrowing, sclerosis, and
osteophytes
Fujiwara et al17 are credited for the standard MRI-based classification of facet degeneration
(Resource 5).
Grade 1: normal
Grade 2: joint space narrowing or mild osteophytes
Grade 3: sclerosis or moderate osteophytes
Grade 4: marked osteophytes
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Obtaining a thorough history is critical in the evaluation of a patient with LBP.
Given the wide range of spinal and extraspinal causes of LBP, surgeons must ascertain key
details regarding the duration, location, and character of a patient’s LBP.
A multipoint review of systems may help pinpoint constitutional symptoms and other
concerning associated issues.

Patient History
Obtaining a thorough history is critical in the evaluation of a patient with LBP (Resource
6). Given the wide range of spinal and extraspinal causes of LBP, surgeons must
ascertain key details regarding the duration, location, and character of a patient’s LBP.
Inciting events or trauma should be noted.
A multipoint review of systems may help pinpoint constitutional symptoms and other
concerning associated issues. Information on associated symptoms as well as
numbness, weakness, radiculopathy, bowel/bladder incontinence, and saddle anesthesia
also should be obtained. Red-flag signs should increase suspicion for LBP and warrant
immediate investigation (Table 3).

Eliciting a patient’s spinal surgery history, including details of the procedure (levels,
instrumentation, etc.) and complications, also is important. Information on employment,
related litigation, work injuries, and other sources of secondary gain, also should be
obtained. Inconsistencies provided by the patient should be noted.

Assessment of concomitant mental health, mood, or psychiatric disorders also is
relevant and may help rule out nonorganic causes of back pain. A patient’s medical and
surgical history must be obtained. Prior abdominal surgery and/or radiation may affect
treatment options and the ability to perform anterior retroperitoneal spine surgery.
A focused patient history may provide clues with regard to the source of pain. Patients
with spinal stenosis will report relief with lumbar flexion. Typically, patients with
discogenic pain report increased symptoms while in a sitting position. Facet-related pain
often is activity related and off of midline.
Physical Examination
A comprehensive lumbar spine examination includes lower extremity myotome, dermatome,
and reflex testing (Figure 2).
Spinal cord compression in the cervical or thoracic spine may go unnoticed by the patient and
may be partially masked by severe LBP. A meticulous neurologic examination will reveal
previously undiagnosed myelopathy.

(Reproduced with permission from Klein JD, Garfin SR: History and physical examination, in

1995, pp 71-95.)


Physical Examination
Any weakness, altered sensation, or abnormal reflex should be noted. Additional
mandatory testing includes provocative tests (Table 4; ie, straight leg raise and femoral
stretch) and assessment of clonus. Spinal cord compression in the cervical or thoracic
spine may go unnoticed by the patient and may be partially masked by severe LBP. A
meticulous neurologic examination will reveal previously undiagnosed myelopathy. A
patient’s gait is important, and gait assessment should be a routine part of the physical
examination. Signs of pain, antalgia, or ataxia should be documented.

Manual palpation may help localize a patient’s pain. Any step-off or mechanical
instability should be noted. Paraspinal muscles should be examined for focal tenderness
or spasm.
The effect of positioning on symptoms also should be noted. Lumbar spine range of
motion may provide key information on the precise cause of a patient’s pain. Pain with
lumbar flexion may localize the disk as the source of pain. Conversely, painful extension,
especially with ipsilateral bending, may localize the facets as the pain generator.
A thorough physical examination also includes assessment of bilateral hip joints.
Frequently, patients report low back or buttock pain that is caused by hip degeneration.
A patient’s body mass index and overall habitus also should be assessed.
The presence of Waddell signs may indicate a nonorganic component to a patient’s
LBP.18 Surgeons should pay particular attention to Waddell signs in patients involved in
litigation or a worker’s compensation claim.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standing AP and lateral radiographs should be the first-line imaging studies obtained to
evaluate the lumbar spine. In patients without red-flag signs or symptoms, radiographs

9/3/26, 7:26 AM
AAOS | Axial Back Pain
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000052
17/41

generally are obtained after 6 weeks of symptoms.

Radiography
Radiographs allow for assessment of coronal and sagittal alignment of the lumbar spine.
Signs of disk degeneration include loss of height, osteophytes, and spurs.
Cortical margins of the vertebral bodies should be inspected for erosive lesions.
Fractures with associated malalignment also may be observed on radiographs. Vascular
calcifications also can be assessed. Surgeons should note transitional anatomy and
ensure consistent nomenclature is applied across imaging studies. In some patients, a
partially sacralized L5 vertebrae may form a pseudoarticulation with the sacrum
(Bertolotti syndrome) and may be the source of LBP.9 The prevalence of such a finding is
approximately 5%.
Dynamic flexion and extension radiographs should be obtained to rule out
spondylolisthesis or instability. Oblique views of the lumbar spine should be obtained if
concern for pars interarticularis fracture or facet pathology exists.
Computed Tomography
CT is ideal for the evaluation of bony anatomy in the lumbar spine.
Bridging osteophytes, subtle fractures, and endplate morphology are best appreciated on CT
scans.

Computed Tomography
Vascular calcifications of the aorta, IVC, and iliac vessels also can be appreciated.
Therefore, CT can be used to assess the appropriateness of anterior-based procedures.
The vacuum phenomenon may be observed within a disk on CT and indicates abnormal
motion/instability. CT also is a valuable imaging modality to assess for fusion and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000052
18/41

pseudoarthrosis. CT is the best imaging modality to evaluate facet joint degeneration. CT
myelography is performed to define patterns of stenosis in patients in whom MRI cannot
be performed (ie, pacemaker/defibrillator).
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate the soft-tissue anatomy of the lumbar spine;
however, MRI generally is not the first imaging study obtained.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI allows for evaluation of disk signal and morphology. Intravenous contrast is used if
concern for infection or malignancy exists (Figure 3).
On T2-weighted MRIs, a degenerative disk will display a hypointense signal (black disk). In
addition, as disks degenerate, the normal annular pattern and distinction from the inner
nucleus are lost, which are best appreciated on axial T2-weighted MRIs. On axial MRIs,
the concavity of the posterior midline portion of the disk often is lost with disk
degeneration. Other MRI findings that are observed in patients with disk degeneration
include Modic type 1 and type 2 endplate changes and high-intensity zones in the outer
anulus.

Other Imaging Studies
Although assessment of bone density does not aid in diagnosis, it is a critical step in planning
surgical treatment for patients with DDD. Bone density is assessed via dual-energy x-ray
absorptiometry or quantitative CT. Osteopenia (T score <-1.0) and osteoporosis (T score <-2.5)
are contraindications to lumbar TDR.12 Knowledge of reduced bone density also aids in
planning a fusion procedure and may inform the use of additional fixation methods (ie,
cement augmentation).
Diskography, in which contrast medium is injected directly into the disk, is controversial but
useful in the work up of a patient in whom DDD is suspected.12 Refinement of techniques and

9/3/26, 7:26 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000052
20/41

criteria, such as avoiding the injection of normal control disks and standardized injection
pressures, recently have occurred because of concerns for advanced degeneration of
previously healthy levels.19 Pain with injection is rated as concordant or discordant. Key
findings include provocation of pain and dye distribution or leakage. Diskography may confirm
that the disk of interest is the primary pain source.4,12
Pathology
Decreased disk height results in altered spinal biomechanics, furthering the degenerative
cascade of the spinal segment.
Radicular symptoms may occur in patients with DDD because of reduced foraminal area,
particularly in the craniocaudal axis. This results in compression of the exiting nerve root at
the affected level (ie, L5 nerve roots at L5/S1).

Pathology
In patients with DDD, the disk undergoes a series of changes that leads to alteration of
the local biology and architecture. DDD is characterized by a decline in proteoglycan
concentration with loss of water content, reduced viable cells, a decrease in pyridinoline
crosslinks, and an increase in pentosidine crosslinks. Pentosidine is a marker of
advanced glycosylation. Decorin and biglycan are observed in relatively increased
concentrations as the disk degenerates.3 Decreased disk height results in altered spinal
biomechanics, furthering the degenerative cascade of the spinal segment.
Radicular symptoms may occur in patients with DDD because of reduced foraminal area,
particularly in the craniocaudal axis. This results in compression of the exiting nerve root
at the affected level (ie, L5 nerve roots at L5/S1).
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of symptomatic lumbar DDD is based on a combination of a thorough patient
history, physical examination, imaging studies, and strategic diagnostic interventions.4

Diagnosis
Diagnosis of symptomatic lumbar DDD is based on a combination of a thorough patient
history, physical examination, imaging studies, and strategic diagnostic interventions.4
The likelihood of asymptomatic degeneration observed on imaging studies is high.
Surgeons must isolate the etiology of a patient’s symptoms. If concern for a considerable
facet component to a patient’s pain exists, then facet blocks are recommended. The
preferred method for the diagnosis of facet pain is a controlled anesthetic block into the
joint or its nerve supply. Other causes of pain should be ruled out before recommending
surgical management for discogenic LBP.
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for acute or chronic LBP includes a wide range of spinal and
extraspinal causes.
Common spine-related causes of LBP include but are not limited to DDD,
instability/spondylolisthesis, Bertolotti syndrome, sacroiliac joint degeneration, annular
tears, facet joint degeneration, muscle/ligament sprain, spinal stenosis, fracture, infection
(discitis/osteomyelitis), inflammatory arthritis, tumors, and sickle cell disease.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management is the mainstay of treatment for patients who have acute LBP
without red-flag signs.

Indications
Initial management consists of relative rest, cessation of pain-generating activity, and a
course of anti-inflammatory medications (if tolerated).

Muscle relaxants can be administered for a short duration if obvious spasm is noted on
physical examination. Adjunctive treatment options include physical therapy and local
modalities (heat, cold, massage, etc.).
Limited evidence exists to support the use of alternative therapies, such as acupuncture
and spinal manipulation. In general, exercise programs are based on improving core
strength and conditioning. Exercise programs can be performed at home or under
supervision. Yoga and Pilates may improve flexibility and aerobic conditioning.
The prescription of opioids for the management of nonspecific axial LBP is not
recommended. Lifestyle modifications may influence LBP and should be encouraged in
specific patients. Smoking cessation and weight loss are associated with relief of LBP.
Targeted injections and interventional procedures may be considered in patients with
recalcitrant LBP. Injections and interventional procedures are minimally invasive and
may be useful in patients with pain that has not improved via nonsurgical management.
However, percutaneous techniques for the management of discogenic pain have largely
proven to be unsuccessful.20 In addition, no high-level studies have been performed to
date. Examples of targeted injections and interventional procedures include epidural
steroid injection, intradiscal injections, and intradiscal neurolysis. Although injections
often are not curative, they may be used to target specific regions (ie, facet joint) and
may help confirm the diagnosis. In addition, they may afford a period of pain relief,
allowing for improved participation in other nonsurgical treatment modalities (Table 5).

Indications
Surgical treatment should be used sparingly and as a last resort for patients with axial back
pain.21
The traditional, preferred surgical treatment option for patients with DDD and persistent,
functionally incapacitating pain in whom nonsurgical treatment fails is arthrodesis and
decompression of stenosis, if necessary.22-31
TDR is a motion sparing alternative to spinal fusion. The primary indication for lumbar TDR is
symptomatic DDD with or without radicular pain.28,31-44
Fusion

Fusion
In theory, fusion targets the pain associated with lumbar disk degeneration via removal
of the disk material and elimination of motion at the affected segments. This may be
accomplished via a variety of approaches and fixation options. Fusion techniques can be
categorized into three general groups: anterior or lateral fusion (stand-alone fusion)
(Figure 5), posterior fusion, and 360° fusion (anterior and posterior fusion).
Devices used in fusion include rod-and-screw posterior constructs; anterior or lateral
interbody spacers; and interbody devices that are inserted via a dorsal approach, such
as transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion. Several fusion approaches have been
described, including the midline posterior approach and the Wiltse approach. Each
device is associated with advantages and disadvantages. Bone graft options include local
or iliac autograft, allograft, or graft substitute.

Proper patient selection is critical to achieving good outcomes with TDR. TDR is primarily
indicated in physiologically younger adults. Patients must be skeletally mature and must
not have substantial axial deformity. LBP should be attributed to DDD at L3-S1, and the
patient should have undergone at least 6 months of unsuccessful nonsurgical treatment.
In addition, the facets at the treatment level should be relatively healthy (Figure 6).

Numerous absolute and relative contraindications to lumbar fusion and TDR have been

Painful conditions not caused by a disk and conditions that compromise long-term device

should be avoided.45,46
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning consists of evaluation of lumbar lordosis and pelvic parameters,
especially for fusion procedures.
Attention is paid to the location and calcification of the great vessels ventral to the spine in
patients undergoing anterior and lateral procedures.
In patients undergoing a lateral lumbar procedure, surgeons must carefully analyze the
position of the femoral nerve, lumbar plexus, and iliopsoas, especially at L4/5. Any concerning
findings may indicate consideration of an alternative approach or procedure.
Patient Positioning
Patient positioning is based on the surgical approach.
In general, percutaneous pedicle screw placement is performed with the patient in the prone
position on a four-post Jackson surgical table.
Anterior lumbar approaches are performed with the patient in the supine position on a
general surgical table with the break just above the surgical level. This allows the surgeon to
extend the level of interest and maximize exposure, especially in patients with collapsed levels.
Lateral fusion procedures are performed with the patient in the lateral decubitus position,
most commonly the right lateral decubitus position via a left-sided approach.
The patient’s hips and knees are flexed to reduce tension on the iliopsoas muscle.
Care is taken to protect all bony prominences and secure the patient.
The patient is strategically placed relative to the surgical table break (reverse orientation) to
aid in exposure of and access to the disk space of interest.

Surgical Approaches
The lateral approach affords access to the anterior column of the spine from the
thoracolumbar junction to L4/5. In general, the lateral approach does not require the
assistance of an access surgeon. After incision, the external, internal oblique, and
transversus abdominus are divided in line with their fibers via blunt dissection. Care is
taken to not damage the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves as they pass between the
oblique muscles. The retroperitoneal space is entered, and the peritoneum is retracted
anteriorly. The iliopsoas can then be directly visualized with the use of Wiley retractors.
Under lateral fluoroscopic guidance, a small, initial dilator is placed over the disk space.
After proper positioning is confirmed, a guidewire is passed to secure the position.
Sequential dilators are passed through the muscle. An expandable, table-mounted
retractor is then placed over the dilators to expose the disk space.
The anterior retroperitoneal approach is used in anterior lumbar interbody fusion and
TDR and generally requires the assistance of an access surgeon.47 The IVC lies on the
right side of the spine and is more friable than the aorta. Therefore, the anterior
retroperitoneal approach generally is performed from the left side. In some patients (eg,
a young individual undergoing an anterior procedure at L5/S1), a right-sided approach is
used to access the spine below the IVC bifurcation. Such an approach allows for
preservation of a clean plane on the patient’s left side should a cranially adjacent-level
procedure be necessary in the future.
Posterior approaches are used in the surgical treatment of patients with DDD who
cannot undergo anterior- or lateral-based procedures.
Postoperative Management
Patients are instructed to avoid hyperextension after TDR. All patients are instructed to avoid
bending at the waist, lifting, or twisting.
With the anterior approach, diet is advanced after the patient has flatus.
Ambulation is strongly encouraged postoperatively. Patients are administered a short course
of narcotic pain medication postoperatively.

Complications
Complications are divided into approach-related, device-related, and patient-related
complications.48

Complications
Approach-related complications include injuries to the major vessels and the ureters and
retrograde ejaculation. In several studies on TDR, approach-related complications were
reported in as many as 10% of patients, which was similar to the rate of approach-
related complications encountered in fusion control groups.28,49
Device-related complications include implant subsidence, migration or extrusion,
malpositioning, and material wear or reaction.27,28,34 Implant subsidence has been
reported in as many as 67% of patients in whom TDR fails.50 Implant subsidence can be
minimized by avoiding TDR in patients with poor bone quality, avoiding endplate
violation intraoperatively, and seating the implants on the more cortical peripheral
edges of the vertebral end plates. The risk of device migration or extrusion substantially
depends on implant design, placement, and sizing.27,40
Patient-related complications include adjacent-level disk degeneration, same-level facet
degeneration, and heterotopic ossification. Successful motion preservation is the main
mechanical goal of lumbar TDR.24,42 Adjacent-segment degeneration observed after
arthrodesis is thought to be related to increased stress at adjacent segments because of
the transfer of extra motion and loads from the fused segment.51

Other Complications
Pseudoarthrosis may occur after any fusion procedure. However, with the use of
modern implants and biologics, current rates of fusion exceed 90%, even after stand-
alone anterior instrumentation.52
Vascular injury and retroperitoneal bleeding are serious complications associated with
the anterior approach. The reported incidence of vascular injury ranges from 1% to
7%.47
Injury to the sympathetic nerves occurs in 2% of patients treated via a retroperitoneal
approach.53 Injury may result in sexual dysfunction, namely retrograde ejaculation.
Neurologic injury to the femoral nerve and lumbar plexus may occur with lateral lumbar
interbody fusion. Patients in whom such injuries occur may experience thigh
dysesthesias, paresthesia, and numbness. These complications often resolve within 1
year. Patients often will have some pain and limited weakness with ipsilateral hip flexion
postoperatively as a result of iliopsoas dissection.
Outcomes
Historically, the outcomes of anterior lumbar interbody fusion, both stand-alone procedures
and procedures with posterior instrumentation, are good; however, good outcomes heavily
rely on proper patient selection.12,23-26,31,54-56

In 2018, Radcliff et al26 published the 5-year secondary surgery rates of patients from
the two-level ProDisc-L FDA investigational device exception study. A total of 229
patients (161 TDR, 68 fusion) were included in the analysis. At final follow-up, patients
who underwent two-level TDR were substantially less likely to undergo secondary
surgery than patients who underwent two-level circumferential fusion (5.6% versus
19.1%); however, most of the secondary surgical procedures in the fusion cohort (65%)
involved instrument removal. After excluding secondary surgery that involved
instrument removal, a substantial difference between TDR and fusion was not reported.
The patients who underwent two-level TDR had a lower rate of secondary surgery for
adjacent segment disease than the patients who underwent two-level circumferential
fusion (2.5% versus 5.9%); however, the difference was not significant. The authors
concluded that two-level TDR is noninferior to two-level circumferential fusion.
Hoff et al57 compared hybrid reconstruction with circumferential lumbar fusion via
transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion. At a mean follow-up of 37 months, all the
patients had substantial clinical improvement; however, the patients who underwent
hybrid reconstruction had substantially better visual analog scale scores at all time
points compared with the patients who underwent fusion. Lumbar lordosis improved in
both groups; however, lordosis changes in the patients who underwent hybrid
reconstruction occurred at the index levels, whereas lordosis changes were localized
proximal to the surgical levels (L1-L4) in the patients who underwent fusion. In addition,
the patients who underwent fusion had substantially increased range of motion at the
adjacent level (L3/4). The authors concluded that hybrid reconstruction resulted in
superior clinical outcomes, with a more balanced restoration of lumbar lordosis.
